parole.significato: atmosphere
parole.testo: Ultimately from New Latin atmosphaera, from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (atmós, “steam”) + Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”)

parole.significato: author
parole.testo: Ultimately from New Latin autor, from Latin auctor. Compare Lithuanian autorius, Polish autor, German Autor.

parole.significato: beryllium (chemical element, atomic number 4)
parole.testo: From New Latin beryllium, from beryllus, from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (bḗrullos, “beryl”), + -ium.

parole.significato: central, central station (main, leading part, usually of some device or system)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately a borrowing from New Latin centrāle, the neuter form of the adjective centrālis

parole.significato: electric, electrical
parole.testo: Ultimately derived from New Latin ēlectricus (“electrical; of amber”) from ēlectrum (“amber”) + -icus (“adjectival suffix”), from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron, “amber”). With -isks ending.

parole.significato: hassium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 108.)
parole.testo: From Hassia, the New Latin form of the name the German state of Hessen, the location of the institute where the element was first synthesized.

parole.significato: chromium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 24)
parole.testo: From New Latin, from French chrome, from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”).

parole.significato: helium (chemical element, noble gas)
parole.testo: From New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”) (because its presence was first theorised in the sun's atmosphere).

parole.significato: calcium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 20)
parole.testo: From New Latin calcium, derived by Sir Humphry Davy in 1808, from Latin calx (“lime, limestone”), because it occurs in limestone.

parole.significato: criterion, criteria (essential characteristics that distinguish entities or phenomena; a test for comparing, distinguis…
parole.testo: Via some other European language, from New Latin criterion, from Ancient Greek κριτήριον (kritḗrion, “a test, a means of judging”), from κριτής (kritḗs, “a judge”), from κρίνω (krínō, “I judge”).

parole.significato: lithium (chemical element, atomic number 3)
parole.testo: From New Latin lithium, from lithia (in reference to Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”)) + -ium, a name created in 1818 by Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius (in Latvian: Jenss Jākobs Bercēliuss) to stress this metal's mineral origin, unlike other previously known alkalis of vegetable origin.

parole.significato: logarithm (power to which a certain base must be raised in order to obtain a given number)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately a borrowing from New Latin logarithmus, a term coined by Scot mathematician John Napier from Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos, “word, reason”) and ἀριθμός (arithmós, “number”).

parole.significato: magnesium (chemical element, a light, silvery metal, with atomic number 12)
parole.testo: From New Latin magnēsium, from Magnēsia (“region in Thessaly”).

parole.significato: microscope (instrument for observing small objects)
parole.testo: Internationalism, from New Latin microscopium (or via some other European language), from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + σκοπέω (skopéō, “to look at”).

parole.significato: molecule (smallest part of an element or compound that still preserves its chemical properties)
parole.testo: From New Latin mōlēcula.

parole.significato: molybdenum (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 42.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin molybdaenum, from Ancient Greek μόλυβδος (mólubdos, “lead”), because the two elements are so similar they were often confused.

parole.significato: national (relating to a nation or people)
parole.testo: From nācija (“nation”) + -āls. Clearly not formed in Latvian, but borrowed as such from some other European language (ultimately from New Latin nationalis).

parole.significato: sodium (chemical element, an alkali metal, with atomic number 11)
parole.testo: From New Latin natrium.

parole.significato: polonium (nonmetallic, sometimes considered metalloid, chemical element, with atomic number 84.)
parole.testo: From New Latin Polonia (“Poland”), Marie Curie's home country.

parole.significato: rubidium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 37.)
parole.testo: A New Latin word derived by German chemist Robert Bunsen in 1861, from Latin rubidus (“red”), because its spectrum has two red lines.

parole.significato: selenium (nonmetallic, sometimes considered metalloid, chemical element, with atomic number 34.)
parole.testo: A New Latin word derived by Swedish chemist Berzelius in 1818, from Ancient Greek σελήνη (selḗnē, “moon”).

parole.significato: scandium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 21)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin scandium, from Latin Scandia (“Scandinavia”).

parole.significato: tantalum (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 73.)
parole.testo: A New Latin word derived by Swedish chemist Anders Gustaf Ekeberg in 1802, from Latin tantalus.

parole.significato: utopia
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from New Latin Ūtopia, the name of a fictional island, possessing a seemingly perfect socio-politico-legal system in the book Utopia (1516) by Sir Thomas More. Coined from Ancient Greek οὐ (ou, “not, no”) + τόπος (tópos, “place, region”).

parole.significato: geology (science that studies the composition, structure, and development of the Earth)
parole.testo: Probably via some other European language, ultimately from New Latin geologia, from Ancient Greek γῆ (gê, “earth”) and λόγος (lógos, “word, study”) + -ija.
